title: It grows
hook: a study tested whether weeks of loving-kindness practice change a person's days

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martin Luther King Jr. on agape. Your line was goodwill for all. Did an opponent get a little of it? Today, a question for the lab: can that kind of love be practiced into being? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

May all beings be happy. That's the heart of an old Buddhist teaching, the Metta Sutta, which describes a love meant to reach every living thing, near and far, seen and unseen. Say a sentence like that, and a fair question comes up. Does saying it change anything in the one who says it? Or is it a lovely sentence that floats away? A team of psychologists decided to find out. They taught a group of working adults a loving-kindness meditation, then followed them week after week, asking each evening how the day had gone inside. Today: what they found, and why the title is only two words.
screen: `MAY ALL BEINGS BE HAPPY.` → `DOES SAYING IT CHANGE ANYTHING?` → `A TEAM DECIDED TO FIND OUT.`

segments.voice: First, a practice, not a mood. In the Metta Sutta, boundless love isn't something that simply happens to a person. The text speaks of cultivating a boundless heart toward all beings, the way a mother guards her only child. Buddhist teachers call metta a practice: you sit, you bring someone to mind, and you wish them well on purpose, whether or not the warmth shows up. Second, the study. Psychologist Barbara Fredrickson and her colleagues ran it. Some participants learned loving-kindness meditation; a comparison group waited their turn for the course. Both groups kept reporting on their days. Over the weeks, the meditators reported more positive emotions in ordinary life, things like joy, gratitude, contentment, hope and love. Third, small days, stacked up. The gains didn't arrive all at once on day one. The paper describes them showing up gradually, as people kept practicing. That's the plain meaning of today's line. Nobody flipped a switch. Something got watered. Fourth, what it built. Fredrickson's larger idea is called broaden and build: good feelings widen what a person notices, and over time they build lasting resources. In the study, the meditators also reported more sense of purpose, more support from others, and more satisfaction with their lives. Now the honest part. This is one study. People reported on themselves, and the changes were modest. It doesn't prove anything about the deep nature of love. But on one plain point it agrees with the old sutta: this kind of love is something a person can grow.
screen: `A PRACTICE, NOT A MOOD.` · `THE STUDY: WEEKS, NOT MOMENTS.` · `SMALL DAYS, STACKED UP.` · `WHAT IT BUILT.` · then, large: `IT GROWS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind someone easy to love: a friend, a grandparent, a pet. Silently offer them the kind of wish the practice uses, something like may you be well, may you be at ease. Let the words go slowly. If warmth comes, fine. If it doesn't, keep going anyway; that's the practice. Stay with this one person the whole time, repeating the wish at the pace of the breath, the way a gardener waters the same bed every day. If you pray, you can hold them before God as you go. The bell holds the time.
It grows. Loving-kindness treated as a practice that strengthens with use, as the Metta Sutta teaches and a modern study set out to test. Today's word.
Your line: it grows. Today, find five minutes for loving-kindness somewhere in the day, and check one thing at the end: was it any easier than at the start? Day eight hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhist meditators practice loving-kindness (metta) by silently wishing well to themselves and others in widening circles, often for a set time each day; the practice is also taught in secular meditation courses and has been studied by psychologists.
